summary: Since 1966, NASA has sent numerous spacecraft, robotic rovers, and research stations to the Moon and Mars. Once their missions conclude, these craft become space debris. This debris contains valuable materials, including aluminum, titanium, gold, and solar panels; recovering these resources for return to Earth would be highly beneficial. To this end, decommissioned machinery could be dismantled and repurposed by robots or solar-powered processing units. Furthermore, any radioactive materials or microbes potentially introduced from Earth must be rendered safe through specialized containment systems. Meanwhile, historically significant artifacts—such as those from the Apollo 11 mission—should be preserved and transformed into open-air museum exhibits. Additionally, rock samples of scientific value should be transported to space stations for detailed analysis. In this way, space debris can be reduced while safeguarding both our historical heritage and the natural integrity of these celestial bodies.
details:
What does it do or how does it work? Our project addresses the sixty-year accumulation of space debris and heritage hardware on the Moon and Mars. Operating as a circular cosmic ecosystem, our system combines solar-powered smelting furnaces (ISRU) that convert the hulls of retired spacecraft into structural materials, autonomous tow rovers and laser shears that dismantle large platforms on-site, armored security vaults for nuclear RTGs and biological quarantine, dust-shielded open-air museums that protect historic milestones, and reusable shuttle systems that transport valuable scientific samples to the Lunar Gateway for advanced microgravity analysis.

What benefits does it have? It eliminates the astronomical fuel costs of returning heavy space wreckage to Earth, provides on-site raw materials for future planetary bases, minimizes biological and nuclear contamination risks, and establishes a sustainable infrastructure for deep space exploration What is the intended impact of the project? To transform retired space missions from silent monuments or dangerous obstacles into the building blocks of tomorrow’s bases, ensuring that humanity can explore space sustainably without leaving permanent environmental scars on celestial bodies

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project? We used PowerPoint and research data from NASA surface missions (such as Surveyor, Apollo, Opportunity, and Perseverance); additionally, we utilized various AI tools for assistance during the project development process.

How is your project creative? Instead of viewing space exploration waste as an end, it treats planetary surfaces as self-sustaining circular economies where yesterday’s retired explorers directly power tomorrow’s infrastructure.

What factors did your team consider? We balanced engineering challenges such as In-Situ Resource Utilization (ISRU) and planetary protection (such as containing nuclear RTGs and Earth microbes)with the necessity of preserving humanity’s historic milestones (through dedicated dust-shielded open-air museum zones).
